Mom, I am not guilty of anything.
You must know how to answer for your actions.
Thank you for the support, Mom.

meanings.note: сто пятьдесят = a hundred and fifty; сто рублей = a hundred roubles

examples.trans: I've got a hundred and ten.

examples.text: Понимаешь, Аркаша, мы все скидываемся на этот кластер. Мне москвичам сегодня надо отдать сто пятьдесят.
examples.trans: You see, Arkasha, we're all chipping in for this cluster. I have to give the Moscow people a hundred and fifty today.

meanings.note: Russian numeral ('sixty') that declines for case and governs case agreement on the counted noun.

examples.text: Давление поднялось почти до ста шестидесяти на девяносто.
examples.trans: Blood pressure rose to almost one hundred sixty over ninety.

examples.text: В главном зале ресторана сегодня накрыли столы на шестьдесят гостей.
examples.trans: In the main hall of the restaurant today tables were set for sixty guests.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'on' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('onto, to; for') (+ accusative: на второй срок) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Russian numeral ('ninety') that declines for case and governs case agreement on the counted noun.

examples.text: У него давление сто шестьдесят на девяносто.
examples.trans: His blood pressure is one hundred sixty over ninety.

examples.text: Этот старинный рецепт знают уже девяносто лет.
examples.trans: This vintage recipe has been known for ninety years already.

meanings.note: pointing at a thing or a situation; 'это' + noun = 'this is ...'
points at something: это моё = that's mine
Secondary conversational sense ('is') (linking word: главное — это народ) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: goes right before the word it negates
Derived feminine noun formed with a productive Slavic suffix, used in spoken Russian to mean 'joke'.

examples.trans: What kind of jokes are these?

meanings.note: 'что я за мэр такой' = what kind of mayor am I
Secondary conversational sense ('? = what's this?') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Verbal action/result neuter noun formed with '-ение'/'-ание'. Common neuter noun meaning 'blood pressure' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Those make your blood pressure rise.

examples.text: Давление? Ничего, от тебя у меня просто кружится голова.
examples.trans: Blood pressure? It's nothing, you just make my head spin.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'very'.
Secondary conversational sense ('very much') (with verbs: очень люблю) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town very much.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Работать с таким острым ножом без привычки очень опасно.
examples.trans: Working with such a sharp knife without practice is very dangerous.

examples.text: Опасно оставлять горячую сковороду с маслом без присмотра на плите.
examples.trans: It is dangerous to leave a hot pan with oil unattended on the stove.

meanings.note: emphatic at the start of a sentence
Secondary conversational sense ('? = really?, oh yeah?') (disbelief) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Russian determiner/pronoun ('all') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('everything') (neuter всё) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('everyone') (plural все) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
the present tense is normally left out: я мэр = I am the mayor
Secondary conversational sense ('there is, there are') (present есть; у меня есть = I have) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
future: буду / будешь ... + infinitive

examples.trans: You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'well'.
Secondary conversational sense ('good, fine') (as an answer) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Хорошо, Виктор Петрович, я сейчас же всё переделаю заново!
examples.trans: All right, Viktor Petrovich, I will redo everything right now!

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'any', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.

examples.text: Любая обезьяна эти выборы выиграет! Ты что, хуже обезьяны?
examples.trans: Any monkey will win this election! What, are you worse than a monkey?

meanings.note: 20th-century borrowing from English 'stress' (ultimately from Old French 'estrece', narrowness/oppression).

examples.trans: Any stress and it will be bad.

examples.text: Я не могу работать в таком стрессе.
examples.trans: I cannot work in such stress.

meanings.note: emphasis: вот поэтому ты и... = that's exactly why you...

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'badly'.
Secondary conversational sense ('it's bad') (predicative) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Послушайте, а можно в другое место? Здесь плохо пахнет.
examples.trans: Listen, could we go somewhere else? It smells bad in here.

meanings.note: Expressive conversational Russian interjection or greeting ('hi') used directly in spoken exchanges.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: мам! = casual 'Mum!' when calling her
Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'how'.
Secondary conversational sense ('as') (как вы знаете = as you know) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Hello! How was it in Hungary?

пройти.gloss: to go through, to pass; to come along

meanings.note: about a feeling or pain: потом пройдёт = it'll pass
'Пройдёмте' = let's go, an official's polite order

examples.text: Пройдёмте, пожалуйста, за мной к вашему столику у окна.
examples.trans: Please come along with me to your table by the window.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('your') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.

examples.text: Я бы на твоём месте подумал.
examples.trans: If I were you, I'd think about it.

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'working', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('worker') (as a noun) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Мы построим кластер. Это тысячи рабочих мест.
examples.trans: We will build the cluster. That means thousands of jobs.

meanings.note: на днях = in the next few days, or the other day

examples.trans: I'll call in the next few days.
Any day now, on the website.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'fine'.
меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'волить'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to fire', forming an aspectual pair with 'увольнять'.

examples.text: Давай мы его уволим, а тебя на его место назначим.
examples.trans: Let's fire him and put you in his place.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'and', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('so, and what about') (starting a question: а жвачку?) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'низить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'demote, lower'.

examples.text: Его вовсе не уволили, а просто временно понизили в должности.
examples.trans: He was not fired at all, just temporarily demoted in rank.

examples.text: Нужно немного понизить температуру в духовке, чтобы корж не сгорел.
examples.trans: We need to lower the temperature in the oven a bit so the cake layer does not burn.

meanings.note: + genitive: ни копейки = not a penny
Secondary conversational sense ('...  = neither... nor') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Пятьсот. А у меня ни копейки.
examples.trans: Five hundred. And I haven't got a penny.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'in' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('into, to') (+ accusative (where to)) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('what') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('that') (conjunction) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('? = well?') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: short forms виноват / виновата / виноваты are used for 'it's my/your fault'

examples.text: Я ни в чём не виноват.
examples.trans: I'm not to blame for anything.

meanings.en: must, need to, it is necessary
meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'it is necessary'.

examples.trans: We need to do even more.

уметь.gloss: to know how to, to be able to

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'меть'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to know how to', forming an aspectual pair with 'суметь'.

examples.text: Эх, Паша, Паша. Ты считать не умеешь.
examples.trans: Oh, Pasha, Pasha. You can't count.

meanings.en: to answer, to reply, to pick up the phone
meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'вечать'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to answer', forming an aspectual pair with 'ответить'.

examples.text: Я вам звоню, а вы не отвечаете!
examples.trans: I call you, and you don't answer!

examples.text: Почему ты не отвечаешь на мои вопросы?
examples.trans: Why aren't you answering my questions?

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'for' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('behind') (+ instrumental) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
refers back to the subject: 'он держит своё слово' = he keeps his word

examples.text: А что я за мэр такой, который держит своё слово?
examples.trans: And what kind of mayor would I be if I kept my word?

meanings.note: Derived masculine noun formed with a productive Slavic suffix, used in spoken Russian to mean 'act'.

examples.trans: I committed a very foolish act.

examples.text: Это был благородный и смелый поступок.
examples.trans: It was a noble and brave deed.

examples.text: Соколов, не делай сейчас таких глупых поступков.
examples.trans: Sokolov, do not do such foolish deeds right now.

meanings.note: спасибо за + accusative = thank you for

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Prefix 'под-' ('under, up to') indicates approaching or supporting from below (stem 'держка'). Common feminine noun meaning 'support, backing' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: There you go! No support at all!
I really need the family's support.
